name: Amira Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me, Dr Patel. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Amira, please. I'm the junior doctor at Market Square Surgery, a family practice in a market town, owned by Dr Shah, who built it up from nothing over twenty-five years. I see about twenty-seven patients a day: farmers' wives, shopkeepers, schoolchildren, a lot of diabetes. On Thursdays the market's on and half my patients pop in between stalls with their shopping bags.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the problem-solving, and I love Dr Shah's way of running a business: tight, careful, every penny accounted for. I use AI every day, for drafting letters, checking guidelines and planning my diabetes reviews, and I've shown Dr Shah how to use it for the rota. What wears me out is the money at home. My husband Ravi is an accountant at a small firm in town, and we're helping his younger brother through university, so we have maybe three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Hmm, I'd be surprised, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool that people expected too much from. At the surgery I'd keep using it where it saves time and say so. Online I don't post much, but I might share a practical tip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's not bad news for me. My job is safe, Ravi's job is safe, and I keep my small edge of being faster with the tools than most juniors. The real worry is just money, the three weeks and his brother's fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep showing Dr Shah ways to save time with the tools, because I want to be a partner here one day. I'd set up an automatic transfer of £100 a month into savings. And I'd ask Dr Shah whether I can take on the practice's diabetes clinic, which pays a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit stretched, but hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does being a partner matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because owning something is different from working for someone. My father ran a small textile shop for thirty years, and he always said a wage is a rope, but a business is a ladder. Dr Shah will retire in about ten years, and I want to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Ravi feel about the money going to his brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He feels it's his duty, and so do I. In our family, the older one helps the younger one up. It just means we're a bit tighter than other young doctors.

I'd keep using it where it **saves time** at the surgery and share practical tips.

The real worry is **money**: three weeks saved and his brother's university fees.
do: Keep showing Dr Shah **time-saving** uses of the tools.
Set up an automatic **£100 a month** savings transfer.
Ask to run the practice's **diabetes clinic**, which pays a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right. And it's Ravi's job, word for word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the practices that adapt will do well, and the ones that don't will be bought up. At the surgery I'd say we should be first in town, not last. I wouldn't want the government picking which tools we use; let practices choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is mostly fine. I'm the one who knows the tools, and Dr Shah needs me. But Ravi's firm does bookkeeping and tax returns, which is checking and writing and planning, and I think they'd stop hiring and maybe let him go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Dr Shah bring in an AI system for the practice's phone and booking, and offer to manage it. I'd sit down with Ravi and plan his move: he could set up his own small business advice service, using the AI tools himself, for the market traders who trust him. And I'd keep the £100 a month going, more if I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried for Ravi, more than for myself. Also a bit excited for the surgery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Ravi feel about going out on his own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. He likes a steady payslip. But half the market traders already ask my husband Ravi for advice for free at the temple, so the customers are there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd help bring in an AI phone system. What happens to the receptionists?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard part. Mrs Kaur on reception has been there nineteen years. I'd want Dr Shah to keep her, doing the things patients need a person for, but in the end it's his business and his decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's frightening, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to move fast and not wait for the government to save us. At the surgery I'd say we should be the practice that uses AI best. Publicly I'd say families and small businesses need to plan for themselves now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's very bad for us. Ravi's job would be gone by 2028, because AGI does everything an accountant does. And my thinking work goes too: the diagnosis, the planning, the letters. Dr Shah would keep me for a while for examinations and procedures, until the robots in 2031, but a junior is the cheapest to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dr Shah straight away to let me run a private health check service on Saturdays for the town's businesses, hands-on, with AI doing the paperwork. My husband Ravi would start his advice service right away, but with AGI I'm not sure anyone pays for advice. We'd go to his parents and ask to move in for a year, and his brother would have to take a student loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like standing on a ladder that's suddenly swaying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ravi's brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we can't pay his fees any more, and I'd hate it. In our family that feels like failing. He'd say it's fine, he's a good boy, but I'd know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government shouldn't save you. Would you take help if it was offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's help to retrain or start a business, yes. Money for nothing, I'd feel uncomfortable. But I'm not proud enough to let my family go hungry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That gives us room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for anyone who wants to work hard and change. At the surgery I'd push to be the most modern practice in the county. I'd say the government should keep out of the way and let practices find what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right, and Ravi would have time. By 2031 I'd be trained and know the tools better than most, and the hands-on work lasts until 2034. Ravi could build his advice business for five years before AGI, and maybe move into something more practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Dr Shah to bring in AI across the practice from 2027, and I'd manage it. I'd start saving properly toward buying into the partnership, maybe £200 a month once our money settles. And Ravi would start his business in the evenings now, while he still has a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a knot. The knot is Ravi.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that knot about money or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. My husband Ravi is proud. If his work goes, he'd feel useless, and I'd rather he moved early than got pushed. I'd also want him to look at something hands-on, maybe property surveying with his cousin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd want a baby in about three years. In this picture I'd still say yes, maybe a year later. You can't put your life on hold forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's almost the same as Dr Shah's retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for people who plan, and I'd say it to everyone at the surgery. I'd say small practices should get ready now and stay independent. I'd say families should plan their own futures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is good for me. By 2036 I could own part of Market Square Surgery, run with AI, with hands-on work safe until 2039. Ravi would have ten years to move, which is plenty for a clever man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save toward the partnership, £200 a month rising each year. I'd help Dr Shah modernise the practice step by step. And we'd have our first baby in about three years, as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A big chain buying up the small practices before my boss, Dr Shah, retires is the real threat to my plan, more than the AI. Chains have money and lawyers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your father about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm climbing the ladder, like he said. He'd ask if the ladder has a computer on it. I'd say yes, Papa, and the computer works for me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Ravi's job and part of mine would go before we could build anything. What would help is cheap loans for young people starting small businesses, and retraining money that goes to real skills. And keeping small practices independent, so people like me can still own one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns these machines. If a few big companies own all the AI, the small practices and the small shops get squeezed. I'd rather own a small thing than work for a giant.

headlineQuote: If a few big companies own all the AI, the small practices and the small shops get squeezed.

Her husband Ravi is an **accountant**, the household's biggest AI risk.
She is **traditional** and market-minded, preferring enterprise and family help to government.
She goes from anxious to **alarmed** with AGI in two years, and **calm** with ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with Ravi's job and part of hers gone before they could build anything.
